jsnvu6-d1e66-d1e103.summary: Incipit rubric announcing the 'divisio literae' of Peter Lombard's Sentences attributed to Durandus, and introducing the first section, the division of the text of Lombard's Prologue.

jsnvu6-d1e66-d1e119.summary: Gives the overall division of Lombard's Prologue according to the rhetorical scheme of the exordium: Lombard renders the reader well-disposed (benevolus), teachable (docilis), and attentive (attentus). The benevolence section is analyzed as a balance of three motivating causes (his desire to serve the Church, God's promised reward and help, the profit of his fellows) against three deterring causes (his lack of talent, the difficulty of the material and labor, the opposition of the envious), the motivating causes revealing charity toward God and neighbor.
claims: Lombard's Prologue is structured by the three goals of the rhetorical exordium: benevolence, docility, attentiveness
Lombard's motivations for compiling the work express charity toward God and utility for neighbor, set against three corresponding deterrents

jsnvu6-d1e66-d1e161.summary: Subdivides the benevolence section of Lombard's Prologue into six ordered steps (alternating motivating and deterring causes, their collection, the victory of the motivating causes, a further motivating and a further deterring cause), and further subdivides the last step on opponents into the cause, evidence, and wickedness of their contradiction, the wickedness being shown from disordered affection, feigned religion, and obstinate contentiousness. Lemmata mark where each part begins.
claims: The benevolence section proceeds in six steps culminating in the victory of motivating over deterring causes
The opponents' wickedness is shown from disordered affection, simulated religion, and pertinacious contention

jsnvu6-d1e66-d1e207.summary: Divides the docility section of Lombard's Prologue according to the four Aristotelian causes of the work—final, efficient, material, formal—with the lemmata at which each begins.
claims: Lombard makes the reader teachable by setting out the four causes of the work

jsnvu6-d1e66-d1e226.summary: Divides the attentiveness section into three grounds—the utility of the work, the depth of its matter, and the orderliness of its procedure—and closes the general division of the Prologue.
claims: Lombard renders the reader attentive by the work's utility, profundity of matter, and orderly method

jsnvu6-d1e66-d1e244.summary: Gives the 'sententia in speciali' of the benevolence section, paraphrasing Lombard's argument step by step: his desire to profit set against lack of talent, the height of the material against confidence in divine aid and promised reward, the victory of zeal for the Church aimed at defending and explaining the faith and manifesting the sacraments, the charity of his fellows, and finally the opposition of the envious, traced genealogically from discord to error to envy to contradiction and characterized by refusal to subject will to reason and Scripture, superstitious novelty, and clamorous contention.
claims: Lombard's zeal for the Church, directed at defense and exposition of the faith and manifestation of the sacraments, overcomes the deterrents
Opposition to the truth arises from discord, which yields error, then envy, then contradiction
The opponents set their own sense above both reason and the authority of Scripture

jsnvu6-d1e66-d1e320.summary: Completes the special exposition of the Prologue: the final cause is twofold (destruction of error and manifestation of truth), the efficient cause twofold (God principally, Lombard instrumentally), the material cause the examples and authorities of the saints, and the formal cause twofold (the forma tractatus, i.e. division of the work, and the forma tractandi, i.e. mode of proceeding); it then explains the attentiveness section through utility (compendium of scattered material), depth of questions, and the prefatory chapter lists.
claims: The work's final cause is the destruction of error and manifestation of truth
God is the principal and Lombard the instrumental efficient cause of the work
The form of the work is twofold: forma tractatus and forma tractandi

jsnvu6-d1e66.summary: A literal division (divisio textus) of Peter Lombard's Prologue to the Sentences, prefixed to Durandus's commentary. It analyzes the Prologue according to the rhetorical exordium—making the reader benevolent, teachable, and attentive—first in general (with lemmata marking each part) and then in special exposition. Benevolence is won by weighing three motivating causes (desire to serve the Church, divine aid and reward, the profit of fellows) against three deterrents (lack of talent, difficulty of material, the envious), the latter's malice traced to disordered will, feigned religion, and contentiousness. Docility comes from the four causes of the work (final: destroying error and manifesting truth; efficient: God and Lombard as instrument; material: patristic authorities; formal: forma tractatus and tractandi). Attentiveness comes from the work's utility, depth, and orderly method.
claims: Lombard's Prologue follows the threefold structure of the rhetorical exordium
The Sentences has God as principal and Lombard as instrumental efficient cause
The work aims at destroying error and manifesting truth through patristic authorities
